anglo-american-axis: The bank that carries out US monetary policy is formally owned by the large commercial banks it supervises and rescues, two of which held nearly three-quarters of its stock in 2018. That stock does not give them control of interest rates, which are set by the Fed's Board and its rate committee, but it does give them seats in the room: they elect six of the New York Fed's nine directors. The 1920s record shows how much of the world's money was steered through a few personal and banking ties between New York and London, outside any vote. For an ordinary reader, the point is that the people closest to the money supply have long been bankers and their partners abroad, not the public. Whether that closeness bends policy today is argued, not proven. The claim that London's merchant banks secretly control the Fed rests on one author and no records.
central-bankers-clubs: Central bankers set much of their common direction in a few small rooms in Basel, Washington and Jackson Hole. Some, like the Group of Thirty, also seat private bankers. The BIS, owned by central banks, cannot be sued in Swiss courts, its assets cannot be seized, it pays no Swiss tax, and no national auditor reviews it. The bank-capital rules written in Basel are then copied into national laws that decide how much your bank can lend and what it must hold in reserve, yet no voter elects the people who draft them. These forums are not secret: their members and reports are public. What a reader cannot see is what is said inside, and who pays for some of them.
cfa-franc-zone: Fourteen African countries and the Comoros use money whose exchange rate and convertibility are guaranteed by France's treasury, a former colonial power. For decades that came with a duty to park at least half their reserves in Paris, and French officials sat on their central banks' boards (in West Africa until 2019). When the currency's value was halved overnight in January 1994, the price of imports in CFA francs doubled for millions of people who had no say in the decision. West Africa won changes in 2019-2020, but the guarantee remains, and Central Africa and the Comoros still deposit reserves in Paris. The arrangement brings price stability, which supporters stress. It also means these countries' central banks cannot set their own money freely.
banknote-printer-bribery: Here central banks were on both sides of the bribe. Firms owned by the central banks of Australia and Austria paid officials at other central banks to win the contracts to print their national money. The client countries' citizens paid the inflated price through their own central banks, and in the Austrian cases the padding was 14-20%. The buyers' officials were almost never named or convicted, and no court found that the owners' boards knew. The pattern shows how the printing of money, which most people never think about, is a private contract market open to the same corruption as arms or construction deals.
finance-revolving-door: Many of the people who set interest rates and supervise banks came from, or went on to, the same handful of firms: Goldman Sachs, Carlyle, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup, BlackRock, Citadel and PIMCO. Officials learn how markets think, and the firms gain people who know how regulators think and whom to call. No source here shows a decision bent for a former or future employer. The worry critics raise is quieter: when rule-makers share careers, contacts and assumptions with the industry they oversee, the industry's view of what is reasonable tends to become the official view. A reader should notice that ordinary depositors and borrowers have no similar path into these jobs.
weaponized-reserves: A country's savings held abroad are only as safe as its relations with the place that holds them. Because so many central banks keep gold and dollar assets at the New York Fed, the Bank of England and Euroclear in Brussels, the US, UK and EU can freeze them, and have done so to Iran, Libya, Afghanistan, Venezuela and Russia. Each freeze had a stated reason: hostage-taking, war or contested government. Each also showed every other country that its reserves can be used as leverage. In Afghanistan's case it left the central bank of a country already in crisis without most of its reserves.
swap-line-blocs: In a crisis, a swap line decides which countries can get dollars quickly and which cannot. The Fed gives standing access to only five central banks, all close allies, and in 2008 it left out countries such as Russia, Turkey, India and Iceland. Those countries had to spend their own reserves or go to the IMF, which attaches conditions such as spending cuts and higher taxes. China now offers a rival network to 32 countries and regions, much of it drawn in rescues. The effect for ordinary people is that whether their country's currency collapses in a panic can depend on its diplomatic standing with Washington or Beijing, not only on its own choices.
gulf-dollar-pegs: Five Gulf states tie their money to the dollar, so their central banks follow the Fed's interest-rate moves whatever their own economies need. After the 1974 oil embargo, Saudi oil earnings were recycled into US government debt under a deal kept secret for 41 years, and into US goods through a joint commission. The arrangement gave the US a steady buyer for its debt and gave the Saudi state security and market access, without public debate in either country. No source here shows a written promise to price oil only in dollars; that popular claim is unproven. The recent Chinese swap lines with the Gulf states show the arrangement is no longer the only option.
independence-law-wave: Most of the laws that now shield central banks from elected governments were passed in a single generation, 1989-1999. Many followed loans from the IMF or the conditions for joining the euro. The shield cuts both ways. It keeps politicians from printing money before elections, but it also moves decisions over jobs, prices and debt away from voters to appointed experts and the international bodies that encouraged the change. The laws record what is written, not what happens. The parallel wave of governor firings shows that governments still reach in when they want to.
banking-crisis-waves: Banking crises arrive in waves that cross borders: Latin America in the early 1980s, Asia in 1997, the US and Europe in 2008. In each wave, central banks lend heavily to failing banks and governments spend public money to rescue them, at a cost of up to 57% of a year's national output in Indonesia. Bank owners and creditors are often protected while taxpayers and depositors bear the losses. The map's cases include central banks accused of hiding losses or choosing which banks to save. The waves show that the rescue machinery is a standing feature of the system, not a one-off emergency.
governor-removal-wave: Laws that make central banks independent do not stop leaders from firing or pressuring their governors when interest-rate decisions go against them. Türkiye replaced its governor four times between 2019 and 2023, during years of high inflation and a falling lira. The US case shows the same tension can reach the world's most important central bank. These removals are the visible part of political influence. The quieter part is that a governor who expects to be fired may decide differently before anyone says a word.
lebanon-financial-engineering: Lebanon's central bank kept the country's money looking stable for years by paying banks high returns to bring in new dollar deposits, which were used to cover earlier promises. Its own accounts hid the losses behind an invented asset, and two of the world's largest audit firms signed them, with qualifications. When it broke, ordinary depositors lost access to their savings while the largest banks had been the largest beneficiaries. Separately, investigators say about $330 million moved through a company owned by the governor's brother in the British Virgin Islands. The case shows how a central bank can run a scheme the public cannot see until it fails, and how offshore shells and auditors can help it last.
city-of-london-offshore: London built the market where dollars are lent outside US rules, and the islands and territories that London represents abroad, such as the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Jersey and Guernsey, are among the world's main places to hide who owns money. Together the UK and ten of them make up more of the world's financial secrecy than the United States, the top-ranked single country. That matters to central banks because looted or bribed money, including in the Lebanese and Nigerian cases on this map, often passes through these places. For ordinary people it means tax and corruption losses in their own country can end up in accounts their governments cannot see into.
big-four-auditors: Most central banks that hire private auditors use the same four firms, which also audit the commercial banks those central banks supervise. An audit tells the public that the accounts are fair. When the same firms check both the rule-maker and those it rules, and sometimes sign off accounts that later prove misleading, as in Lebanon, the public's main independent check is less independent than it looks. Concentration in four firms is true of the whole audit market and is not proof of influence. It does mean a small number of private partnerships stand between central banks' books and the public.
